reason: The court applied Partition Law section 25(2) as the governing default-party rule, while finding leave to receive the evidence was implied on these facts.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal by applying Registration of Documents Ordinance section 14 priority to the appellant's improperly continued registration.
The rule is the court's holding on mandatory section 19(2) procedure, but the selected quote only says dismissal cannot be sought and does not itself state the procedure.
The quoted functus officio reasoning supports the point, but the statement omits the court's material caveat that the first order must have been legal and valid.
The court quashed the quit notice after holding that Article 140 review may test the legality and reasonableness of the basis for the competent authority's State-land opinion.
The court did hold that the partition interlocutory order required leave under Civil Procedure Code section 754, but the selected quote merely frames the issue.
The court adopted the application test and dismissed the appeal because success on the application would only have allowed the partition trial to continue.
The quote is expressly from Kandaiah v Seenitamby and the appeal was decided on the deeded right of way rather than a fresh prescriptive-servitude holding.
The approbate-and-reprobate rule was part of the court's reasoning, but Civil Procedure Code section 772 was not the provision construed for that rule.
The court dismissed the prescription claim by applying Prescription Ordinance section 3 and the heavy burden on a claimant against paper title.
The statement reflects the court's section 3 prescription analysis, but the quote only concerns ouster and the mapped statute is Evidence Ordinance rather than Prescription Ordinance.
The acceptance principle was material to the deed-of-gift issue, but the cited statute field points to the later revocation statute rather than the rule on acceptance.
The court relied on Partition Law section 18(2) to treat the commissioner's report as evidence without further proof subject to calling him as a witness.
The adverse-possession principle was applied to reject the claim, but the supporting quote is a quotation from De Silva v Commissioner General of Inland Revenue.
The court used Partition Law section 26(2)(d) and (g) to reject the argument that leaving shares unallotted defeated the partition action.
The burden under Trusts Ordinance section 83 was central, but the rule drops the statute's material attendant-circumstances qualification.
The court stated the co-owner possession point, but expressly tied the consequence to the unique facts and the need for a partition action rather than a declaration action.
The plaintiff's initial burden in rei vindicatio was the decisive basis for setting aside judgment and dismissing the action.
The court held pending civil proceedings do not bar section 66 proceedings, but the statute field maps to Prevention of Frauds rather than the Primary Courts' Procedure Act.
The court applied the proposition to uphold the Primary Court order, but the supporting quote is expressly from Ananda Sarath Paranagama rather than this judgment's own statement.
The court dismissed the revision application by holding that partition settlements are permissible where all interested parties are before court and participate.
The statement is a fact-specific conclusion on a substitution challenge, while the selected quote is only the final dismissal and section 394(2) is not the rule stated.
The court dismissed writ relief because the dispute was private and fact-heavy, but the supporting quote is from Mendis rather than this court's own holding.
The court allowed the writ after holding that possession and long lease of State land without the stipulated procedure was ultra vires and offended public trust.
The quote supports one decisive defect, but the rule omits the related urgency and evidentiary conditions and the actual provision construed was section 38 rather than section 2.
